report.source_text: A 46-year-old man, with hypertension and past history of cigarette smoking, presented to the emergency department (ED) on March 26 for symptoms consistent with upper respiratory infection (cough, sore throat, and fever). The patient had been put on azithromycin by the general practitioner 3 days before the presentation in the ED. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assay on nasal-pharyngeal swab sample was negative for SARS-CoV-2, while a chest X-ray was reported as suggestive for mild interstitial pneumonia. Thus, the patient was hospitalized in a COVID-19 ward and eventually discharged 3 days after, afebrile and without signs of respiratory dysfunction.

report.source_text: A few days after discharge, the patient suffered from shortness of breath, generalized weakness, and marked effort intolerance. Moreover, he occasionally found low values of arterial oxygen saturation on self-measurement at home (O2 saturation swinging from 91–97% over the day). For this reason, he presented to ED again on April 4, when another nasal-pharyngeal swab PCR for SARS-CoV-2 was negative. The chest CT scan showed modest bibasilar infiltrates (Fig. 1), and the arterial blood gases were within normal values.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 46-year-old man with hypertension and smoking history presented to the ED on March 26 with upper respiratory infection symptoms (cough, sore throat, fever). SARS-CoV-2 PCR was negative, but chest X-ray showed mild interstitial pneumonia. He was hospitalized in a COVID-19 ward and discharged on March 29 afebrile without respiratory dysfunction. A few days after discharge (around April 1-3), he developed shortness of breath, generalized weakness, marked effort intolerance, and fluctuating oxygen saturation (91-97%). He returned to the ED on April 4 with negative SARS-CoV-2 PCR and modest bibasilar infiltrates on chest CT, but normal arterial blood gases. Given persistent fatigue and dyspnea with only mild CT findings, neurological evaluation was requested. On April 24, the neurologist documented classic signs of neuromuscular fatigability: hypophonia after sustained speech, diplopia, ptosis on sustained upward gaze, and proximal lower limb weakness (4/5 MRC scale), with normal deep tendon reflexes. Serological testing for anti-AChR, anti-MuSK, and anti-RyR antibodies was negative (seronegative MG). Repetitive nerve stimulation EMG showed a 15% decrement in the amplitude of compound muscle action potential in the right nasalis muscle at 5 Hz stimulation, confirming neuromuscular junction dysfunction. Chest CT review showed no thymic residual tissue, ruling out thymoma. The clinical presentation, neurological examination findings, and electrophysiological evidence of decremental response on RNS EMG established the diagnosis of seronegative generalized myasthenia gravis.

Few days after discharge, patient developed shortness of breath, generalized weakness, marked effort intolerance, and fluctuating O2 saturation (91-97%)
On April 4, patient returned to ED with negative SARS-CoV-2 PCR, modest bibasilar infiltrates on CT, and normal ABG
On April 24, neurologist documented hypophonia with sustained speech, diplopia, ptosis on sustained upward gaze, proximal lower limb weakness (4/5 MRC), and normal deep tendon reflexes
Neurological evaluation was requested to rule out neuromuscular condition given fatigue and dyspnea with only mild CT findings
Serological testing for anti-AChR, anti-MuSK, and anti-RyR antibodies was negative
Repetitive nerve stimulation EMG showed 15% decrement in amplitude of compound muscle action potential in right nasalis muscle at 5 Hz stimulation
Chest CT review showed no thymic residual tissue identified

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: SARS-CoV-2 PCR negative on both March 26 and April 4
Chest CT review showed no thymic residual tissue identified
Serological testing for anti-AChR, anti-MuSK, and anti-RyR antibodies was negative, consistent with seronegative MG

remaining_uncertainties: Exact timeline of symptom onset for ptosis, diplopia, and hypophonia between March 29 discharge and April 24 neurologist evaluation
Whether patient was hospitalized between April 4 and April 24
Specific anticholinesterase or immunosuppressive medications prescribed and dosing
Clinical response to treatment and functional status at discharge or final follow-up
Whether respiratory symptoms during initial hospitalization or April 4 ED visit had MG component (myasthenic crisis consideration)

evaluation.known_final_diagnosis: strongly supporting a diagnosis of generalized myasthenia gravis (MG)
